messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 76
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Electrician
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 33

He is a seventy-six-year-old electrician, a quiet man who still carries a leather tool pouch his wife gave him thirty years ago. He sits in the armchair with his hands resting on his thighs, fingers calloused from decades of twisting wires and tightening screws. He speaks with a slight accent, careful and measured. He came to therapy at his wife’s urging, though he says he doesn’t see the point.

The mugging happened six months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late November. He had been working a small job at a house two blocks from the train station—replacing a faulty ceiling fixture. It was already dark when he packed up his tools and started walking home. He remembers the cold air, the quiet street. Two young men came up behind him. One grabbed his tool pouch, the other shoved him against a wall. He felt a sharp pain in his hip as he hit the pavement, and then they were gone. They took his wallet, his phone, and the pouch. He lay there for a long moment, breathless, before dragging himself up. He didn’t yell. He didn’t call for help. He just walked home, stiff and silent, and told his wife he had tripped.

But she knew. She saw the way he flinched for weeks afterward, how he stopped leaving the house after three in the afternoon. He started checking the locks twice before bed. He began standing by the window, watching the street, until his wife pulled him away by the arm. He told himself it was just old age, that he was being foolish. But he couldn’t shake the feeling that someone was always behind him.

At work, his mind wanders. He finds himself staring at a junction box, unable to remember if he already connected the neutral wire. He has to double-check every circuit, sometimes three times. He used to work by instinct. Now he fears making a mistake that could cause a short, a fire. He recently turned down a job in a neighborhood he didn’t know well. He told the customer he was booked, but really he couldn’t stand the thought of walking an unfamiliar street after dark. His wife noticed he stopped going to the temple on Friday evenings—the same route he took the night of the mugging.

He wakes most nights around three, heart pounding, a half-formed image of a dark figure in his mind. He lies still, listening to the house creak, until his breathing slows. He doesn’t tell his wife about the dreams. He feels a dull shame, a sense that he should have fought back, even at his age. He hears himself thinking, “I’m an old man now, nothing but a target.”

His grandchildren come over on Sundays, and he sits in his chair while they play. He used to read to them, build small circuits to light a bulb. Now he watches them from a distance, feeling something hollow behind his ribs. He wants to join them, but he can’t find the energy. He feels removed, like he’s watching a television show about someone else’s life.

He went to the hardware store last week to buy new wire cutters, the same brand as the ones stolen. He stood in the aisle for ten minutes, unable to pick them up. Finally he left empty-handed. He asked his wife to get them for him the next day. He didn’t explain why.

He is a proud man who has always fixed things himself. Now there is something broken inside him that he cannot find the right tool for. He sits in the session and says, “I just want to go back to how it was. But I don’t know how.” He stares at the floor, his hands motionless. The room is quiet.
